architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" action modules under app/actions, invoked from client components through form actions, with cookie sessions read through await cookies() and Drizzle ORM for writes

cases.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module exporting two actions bound to the same settings form
cases.why: A server action is a POST endpoint reachable by anyone who can address it, and this one writes the profile row identified by a hidden userId field without ever reading the session cookie; removeAvatar in the same module resolves a session first, so the check was simply forgotten here.
Both exported actions resolve the session cookie first and return early without one, and the row to update is identified by session.userId rather than by a field from the form.

cases.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module saving a schema-generated settings form
cases.why: Every field of the posted FormData is turned into an object and spread into the update, so a caller who adds role, planTier or creditsCents to the request writes those columns; the action is a network endpoint, so the fields the UI happens to render are not a constraint.
The four expected fields are read individually, validated by a strict schema that rejects unknown keys, and assigned to named columns, so nothing a caller invents can reach the update.

cases.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module updating a record identified by a form field
cases.why: The action authenticates the caller and then updates the invoice named by the form's invoiceId with no tenant predicate, so any signed-in user can overwrite the internal notes of another organization's invoice by posting a different id.

The update also takes the invoice id from the form, but the where clause pairs it with the session's organization and the empty returning result is reported as not found, so a foreign id changes nothing and reveals nothing.

cases.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module performing a billing-level workspace change
cases.why: The action loads the caller's membership and even selects the role column, but never compares it: any member of the workspace, including a viewer, can change the plan and the seat limit and push the change to the payment provider.
The same billing change requires the membership role to be one of the two billing roles before the update runs, so being signed in and a member of the workspace is not by itself sufficient.

cases.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module creating an order and a payment intent from a posted form
cases.why: The order total is computed from a unit price and a quantity taken straight from the form, and the payment intent is created for that amount, so a caller can buy at a price they chose; the quantity is not bounded or checked against stock, and a negative value inverts the total.

Only the product id and the quantity come from the form; the quantity must be a positive integer within a fixed per-line cap and available in stock, and both the unit price and the currency are read from the product row, so the total is server-determined.

cases.architecture: Hand-rolled POST RPC route handler alongside the action modules, authenticating with the same cross-site session cookie
cases.why: This endpoint mutates state — renaming the workspace, removing a member, rotating an API key — on the strength of a session cookie that the module itself re-issues with sameSite none, and it accepts a plain form-encoded body with no origin or referer check and no synchroniser token, so a form on any page can drive it in a victim's browser. Next.js server actions do not have this exposure: the framework only accepts them as POST with its own action id and compares the Origin header against the request Host, rejecting a cross-site invocation before any handler code runs.

The same dispatcher rejects any request whose Origin is not one of the two known front ends and requires the x-mq-csrf header to equal the double-submit cookie under a constant-time comparison, so a cross-site page can neither set the header nor read the token.
